summary: Describes a sub-delegation of the ietf URN namespace for registered protocol parameters. The ietf namespace from RFC 2648 gives lasting names to IETF-defined things, and this adds a branch for registered items. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: A URN (Uniform Resource Name) is a label that identifies something permanently rather than pointing at where to fetch it. IANA keeps registries of protocol values such as port numbers and media types. RFC 3553 creates a branch of the IETF URN name tree, called params, so that every registered item can be given a name that never changes meaning.

questions: what is the ietf urn namespace
how do i register an iana parameter as a urn
subtitle: Gives IANA-registered protocol parameters stable URN names under urn:ietf:params.

tldr.problem: Standards often need to refer to registered protocol items as URIs, and doing that in an ad hoc way had led to interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC creates a sub-delegation called params below the ietf URN namespace, and sets a template that a registry fills in, put in the IANA considerations section of the specifying document.
tldr.outcome: Registered items get names that never change meaning, such as urn:ietf:params:dns:rr-type-codes:soa, though no resolution mechanism is defined.

facts.label: Template fields
facts.value: 4: Registry name, Specification, Repository, Index value

today: RFC 3553 is a Best Current Practice, BCP 73, published in June 2003. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the naming scheme only; the document itself states that no resolution mechanism is defined.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
From time to time IETF standards require the registration of various protocol elements in a well known central repository. The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority maintains this central repository and takes direction from the IETF on what, how and when to add items to it. The IANA maintains lists of items such as all assigned port numbers, MIME media types, enterprise numbers, and so on.

Over time there has developed a need to be able to reference these elements as URIs in various schemas. In the past this was done in a very ad hoc way that easily led to interoperability problems. This document creates a new sub-delegation below the "ietf" URN namespace called params, which acts as a standardized mechanism for naming the items registered for IETF standards. Any assignments below that are specified in an RFC according to the IETF consensus process and which include the template found in Section 4.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: A URN (Uniform Resource Name) is a label that identifies something permanently rather than pointing at where to fetch it. IANA keeps registries of protocol values such as port numbers and media types. RFC 3553 creates a branch of the IETF URN name tree, called params, so that every registered item can be given a name that never changes meaning.

sections.title: The params Sub-namespace
sections.content:
The sub-namespace name is params, and the declared registrant of the namespace is the Internet Engineering Task Force. The relevant ancillary documentation is the URN syntax specification, the IETF URN namespace specification and the URN namespace definition mechanisms specification.

The namespace is primarily opaque. IANA, as operator of the registry, may take suggestions for names to assign, but it reserves the right to assign whatever name it desires, within guidelines set by the IESG. The colon character is used to denote a very limited concept of hierarchy. If a colon is present, the items on both sides of it are valid names. In general, a name with a colon means the item on the left is a class that contains items of that class. A name can be assigned to an entire list of DNS resource record type codes as well as to each individual code.

For identifier uniqueness, the IESG uses the IETF consensus process to ensure that sub-namespaces generate unique names within that sub-namespace, and delegates to IANA the task of ensuring that the sub-namespace names themselves are unique. Until and unless the IESG specifies differently, IANA ensures uniqueness by comparing the name to be assigned with the list of previously assigned names, and in the case of a conflict requests a new string from the registrant until the conflict is resolved.

For identifier persistence, once a name has been allocated it MUST NOT be re-allocated for a different purpose. The rules for assignments within a sub-namespace MUST be constructed so that the meaning of values cannot change, and the registration mechanism is not appropriate for naming values whose meaning may change over time. If a value changes over time, the assignment MUST name the container or concept that contains the value rather than the value itself.

Identifiers are assigned only after a particular protocol element or number has been registered with IANA using standard policies and procedures, or documented in an RFC describing a standards track protocol. At this time no resolution mechanism is defined. Lexical equivalence is achieved by exact string match according to the rules for URN syntax, and due to the URN syntax definitions the stringprep standard does not apply. There are no additional characters reserved and there is no validation mechanism. The scope is Global.
sections.plainLanguage: The new branch is called params, and the IETF owns it. Names are mostly opaque strings, and a colon separates a class from the items inside it. Once a name is given out it never changes meaning, and the document defines no way to look a name up.

sections.title: Assigning Names
sections.content:
The creation of a new registry name is simple for most flat registries. The only required elements are the registry name, a reference to relevant documents, a statement about which current or proposed document repository contains the authoritative data for the registry, and a statement specifying which element in the registry is the value to be used in the URN. In most cases that last element will be the index value assigned by IANA.

More complex registries, DNS parameters for example, need to repeat that information for any sub-namespaces. It should also be clear whether or not a name is assigned to the sub-namespace itself, that is, whether urn:ietf:params:dns:rr-types is valid by itself and, if so, what it names.

The document gives a template with four fields. Registry name is the name of the sub-namespace, which in many cases should be the same name IANA calls the registry itself. Specification is the relevant IETF published documents that define the registry and the items in it. Repository is a pointer to the current location of the registry in the protocol parameters repository or the relevant RFCs that document the items being named; this value will change over time and is a hint to IANA for the initial mapping rather than a permanent binding to a filename. Index value describes how a registered value is to be embedded in the URI form. This MUST include details of any transformations needed for the resulting string to conform to URN syntax rules, and any canonicalization needed so that the case-sensitive string comparison yields the expected equivalences.

The process for requesting that a URN be assigned is currently to put the template, or a reference to it, in the IANA considerations section of the specifying document. Other, more automated processes may be proposed later if demand requires it.
sections.plainLanguage: Whoever defines a new registry fills in a template with four things: the name of the registry, the documents that define it, where the registry lives, and which value from the registry goes into the URN. The template goes in the IANA considerations section of the document that defines the registry.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: There are no security considerations beyond those already inherent in using URNs. Security considerations for URNs in general can be found in RFC 2141. Further security considerations for one specific URN resolution method can be found in Dynamic Delegation Discovery System Part Four, the URI Resolution Application, which is part of a series starting with Dynamic Delegation Discovery System Part One.
sections.plainLanguage: These names add nothing to the security of URNs themselves. The usual rules for URNs apply.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The document puts a new and significant burden on IANA, since it may require an additional assignment process to happen for each new IANA registry. To minimize the administrative burden on IANA, any parameter namespace registration is very clear about the criteria for inclusion in that namespace.

Defining a registry that fits the constraints of a URN namespace imposes extra discipline, and the document says this should take some of the guess-work out of creating and maintaining that registry.
sections.plainLanguage: Every registry that wants URN names adds work for IANA. The document accepts that, and says the naming rules should make the extra work easier rather than leaving it to guesswork.
